_comment: Host-target registry for the bConnect-MCP guided installer.
The servers in this suite are ordinary stdio JSON-RPC MCP servers plus one
Streamable-HTTP gateway. Nothing in them is specific to any vendor. The only
vendor-specific thing in an install is WHICH FILE gets written and IN WHAT SHAPE.
This file is that knowledge, as data, so an emitter cannot disagree with a
document and so a new host is a JSON entry rather than a code change.
Every 'shape' below was read out of the host's own current documentation on
2026-08-01; the URL is in docUrl and what could NOT be confirmed is in
'unverified'. Where the documentation contradicts itself (Cursor marks `type`
required in a table and omits it from every example) the emitter follows the
VENDOR'S OWN EXAMPLES, because those are what the vendor actually ships against.
id            stable key; what -Hosts takes
rank          the ONE place the selection order lives. 1 first. The array is
kept in rank order too, so the engine's -ListHosts table and the
wizard's list agree without either of them sorting differently.
The order is how likely a baramundi customer is to use the host:
these are overwhelmingly Microsoft estates, so both forms of
Copilot lead -- VS Code for a developer, Copilot Studio for an
automation builder -- and the generic fallback is always last.
It is NOT alphabetical and NOT the order support was added.
transport     stdio | http | both -- what this host can consume from us
mode          merge-json  in-place merge of an existing config file, backed up,
unmanaged content deep-compared, restored on mismatch
THE SYNTAX IS `format`, NOT THE MODE NAME. `codex` is a
merge-json target whose format is `toml`. The name is
historical and it is kept deliberately, because four
PowerShell front ends branch on this field and the
branch that is NOT merge-json DELETES the file whole on
uninstall (Install-BConnectMcp.ps1, the `mode -ne
'merge-json'` test). That is correct for a snippet or a
block file this installer wrote from nothing. It would
be catastrophic for ~/.codex/config.toml, which holds
the operator's model, approval policy, profiles and
every other MCP server they have configured. Renaming
this to `merge-toml` is one line here AND a change in
Install-BConnectMcp.ps1, bconnect.ps1 and State.psm1.
Do all of them or none of them; a guard in
lib\test-host-emitters.mjs fails if this one moves alone.
write-file  a standalone file this host reads; safe to create whole
snippet     we cannot own the target file (YAML we would have to
re-serialise, or a setting typed into a web UI), so we
emit exactly what to paste and where
mode is also what decides whether an install CONFIGURES a host or
only HANDS THE OPERATOR SETTINGS: merge-json and write-file put a
file where the host reads it; snippet cannot, and produces settings
to apply in that product's own interface. The wizard shows that
distinction on every row, before anything is selected, because
four snippet targets (copilot-studio, openai, n8n, open-webui) also
carry serversKey: null and two of them sit near the top of rank.
verification  what the installer can actually PROVE on the machine it runs on:
host-loaded   the host application itself was made to read it here
config-spawn  the emitted file was parsed back and every server in
it started, handshook and served a real bMS read
using the command/args/env from that file. This does
NOT prove the host app loads it.
schema-only   shape-checked against the documented schema. Nothing
was executed. Say so out loud.
unverified    claims deliberately NOT made. Read this before trusting a target.

targets.label: VS Code (GitHub Copilot agent mode)
notes: The top-level key is `servers`, NOT `mcpServers`. This is the single most
common way a hand-copied Claude config fails silently in VS Code.
The file may also carry `inputs` (prompted values, referenced as
${input:id}) and `sandbox`. We never touch those keys; they are preserved.
settings.json is NOT a server-config location -- only behaviour settings
(chat.mcp.access, chat.mcp.discovery.enabled, ...) live there.
unverified: The absolute Windows path of the USER-profile mcp.json. The docs open it
via the 'MCP: Open User Configuration' command and never state a path.
%APPDATA%\Code\User\mcp.json is a plausible guess and is NOT used as a
default here. Pass -HostPath vscode=<path> if you want the user file.

targets.label: Microsoft Copilot Studio
notes: READ THIS BEFORE PLANNING AROUND IT. Copilot Studio has no stdio path at
all, supports Streamable HTTP only (SSE support ended August 2025), and
reaches your server through Power Platform connectors -- meaning the call
originates in Microsoft's cloud. A loopback or private-only gateway is
unreachable by construction.
Neither MCP documentation page mentions the on-premises data gateway,
VNet integration, or any other private-network path. Absence of a
documented path is not proof one cannot exist, but it is not something to
plan a production integration around either.
So the honest options are: publish the gateway through a TLS-terminating,
AUTHENTICATING reverse proxy on a public name, or use a tunnel. Both mean
an internet-reachable path to a component whose own authentication is ONE
shared bearer token (SEC-7): enough to stop a scan, not enough to be the
only control on an internet-facing endpoint -- it does not expire, does
not name a caller, and cannot be revoked for one consumer. Read the
gateway security section in INSTALL.md before doing either.
We emit the custom-connector Swagger skeleton -- the marker that makes it
MCP rather than REST is x-ms-agentic-protocol: mcp-streamable-1.0 on a
POST operation -- and the wizard steps, and nothing else.
CORRECTION 2026-08-01, from the estate owner: baramundi ships a Gateway
utility, deployed on a separate gateway server, which already facilitates
bConnect API calls from off-network and cloud locations. That changes the
shape of this problem and the paragraphs above understate the options.
It means the MCP servers need NOT run on the bMS LAN. Point
BCONNECT_BASE_URL at the baramundi Gateway (BCONNECT_CA_CERT_PATH is there
if it presents its own certificate) and the servers -- and the MCP gateway
in front of them -- can live in a DMZ, a cloud VM or a container. The chain
becomes: Copilot Studio -> MCP gateway -> MCP servers -> baramundi Gateway
-> bMS. "Unreachable by construction" no longer holds.
What it does NOT solve is authentication, and that is still the blocker.
The baramundi Gateway secures the bMS end of the chain; the MCP gateway
authenticates callers with one shared bearer token (SEC-7), which is a
second layer, not a replacement for a proxy: no expiry, no identity, no
per-consumer revocation, and on plain HTTP it is readable in transit. So
wherever you place it, if Microsoft cloud can reach it then it must sit
behind something that terminates TLS and authenticates a PERSON. Do not
read the reachability fix as a security fix -- they are different ends of
the same path.
unverified: Everything about this target is documentation-derived. Nothing was
executed, and no private-network path was found to test.

targets.label: OpenAI Codex (CLI and IDE extension)
activation: Start a new Codex session, or reload the IDE window, so the file is read again.
A session that was already running keeps the configuration it started with.
notes: The first target this installer configures for OpenAI. The other one --
`openai`, the Responses API and Agents SDK -- is a snippet and always will
be, because OpenAI's servers make that call and the endpoint has to be
reachable from the public internet. Codex is the opposite: a local process
spawned over stdio, no gateway, no inbound anything, and a file on this
machine that can simply be written.
The file is TOML, not JSON, and it is the only TOML target here. The
transport is inferred from WHICH KEY IS PRESENT -- `command` means stdio,
`url` means streamable HTTP -- and a table carrying keys from both is
rejected. There is no `type` field to set and setting one would be wrong.
Per-server environment is a `[mcp_servers.<name>.env]` sub-table, so the
capability gates (ALLOW_WRITE_OPERATIONS, ALLOWED_WRITE_TOOLS,
BCONNECT_ENABLE_V11) are carried exactly as they are for the JSON targets,
under the same allowlist. Codex also takes an `env_vars` array for passing
local variables through; this installer does not emit one, because the
credential belongs in the file the --env-file argument points at.
MERGING, WHICH IS THE RISK. This is a file the OPERATOR owns: their model,
their approval policy, their profiles, and any other MCP server they have
configured. So it is spliced, not re-serialised -- the table sections that
are ours are replaced and every other line is carried across unchanged, in
order, comments and all. Three shapes are refused outright rather than
guessed at: `mcp_servers` written as a top-level inline table, an
`[[mcp_servers...]]` array of tables, and one of our server names already
defined as an inline key inside a bare `[mcp_servers]` table. Each of those
would need the whole file re-serialised to edit safely, and this installer
does not re-serialise a file a human wrote.
Project scope: `.codex/config.toml` beside a project also works, for trusted
projects only. Pass -HostPath codex=<path> to write there instead.
READ THIS ABOUT THE LABEL. OpenAI's documentation says the Codex CLI, the
IDE extension and the ChatGPT desktop app all read this same file, and that
configuring it once covers all three. The label names only the two surfaces
that are unambiguously local-process hosts, because a shared configuration
file and a shared ability to RUN a local stdio server are two different
claims and only the first is documented. See `unverified`.
unverified: Whether the ChatGPT desktop application will START a local stdio MCP server
from this file. OpenAI's page says the three surfaces share the file; other
reporting says the consumer ChatGPT app cannot run local stdio servers
without OpenAI's tunnel product. Both can be true at once -- one config
file, different execution limits per surface -- and nothing here can settle
it, because the ChatGPT desktop app is not installed on the machine that
generated this. So the file is written, and no claim is made about which
surfaces then run the servers in it.
The HTTP form. Codex reads a `url` key as streamable HTTP, and this target
deliberately declares stdio only. Codex authenticates an HTTP server with a
bearer token named through `bearer_token_env_var`, this installer never
writes a token into a host config, and a url emitted without one would
produce a 401 from the gateway that an operator could not diagnose from the
file they were handed. stdio needs no gateway and no token, so it is the
only form emitted.
The splicer identifies a table by a line whose first non-blank character is
`[`, tracking multi-line strings so a header inside a triple-quoted value is
not mistaken for one. A `[mcp_servers.x]` written INSIDE somebody's
multi-line prompt template, in a file that also uses the four-quote form of
a multi-line string ending in a quote, is the one construction that has not
been proved to round-trip.

targets.label: Claude Desktop
targets.quitEvidence: observed 2026-08-06: three consecutive runs wrote and verified this file, then it reverted within ~90s of the app starting; a fourth run with zero claude.exe processes held
notes: The original and only target before this feature existed. Written by
lib\merge-config.mjs, which is deliberately NOT shared with the other
targets: that path is verified, in production here, and must not move.
MUST NOT BE RUNNING WHILE THE FILE IS WRITTEN. The app rewrites this file
from its own state at startup, discarding what is there. Quit it (tray
icon -> Quit; a window close leaves it running), confirm no claude.exe
remains -- it runs many processes at once -- and start it only AFTER the
run finishes. Quitting and relaunching BEFORE the run is what fails, and
it fails silently: the run reports success and the app shows no servers.
The earlier wording here said 'full quit and relaunch', which described
exactly the sequence that reproduced the failure twice.
unverified: Whether this file accepts remote/HTTP server entries. Claude Desktop's
remote-server story is Connectors/Extensions, not this file. We do not
emit an HTTP entry here and do not claim one would work.

targets.label: Claude Code (CLI)
notes: Project scope: .mcp.json in the project root, shared via version control.
User scope (~/.claude.json, all projects) and local scope (~/.claude.json
under projects.<path>.mcpServers) exist too; this installer writes project
scope because it is the one that is a small, self-contained file we can
merge without touching unrelated session state.
Precedence is local > project > user; entries are not merged across scopes.
A url entry with no "type" is a documented configuration ERROR -- Claude
Code reads a type-less entry as stdio. The emitter always writes "type".
VERIFIED HERE, 2026-08-01: `claude mcp list` run in a directory carrying an
emitted .mcp.json enumerated both servers and printed their exact command
lines back. It then reported them as 'Pending approval (run `claude` to
approve)' -- project-scope servers need a one-time in-app trust decision
before they are started. That is a deliberate security control, not a
configuration fault, and it is the reason 'host-loaded' here means Claude
Code PARSED the file rather than that it has run the servers unattended.
unverified: The exact top-level skeleton of user scope in ~/.claude.json is described
in prose but not printed verbatim in the docs, so this installer does not
write user scope.

targets.label: OpenAI (Responses API / Agents SDK)
notes: Two different products, and the difference decides whether this is easy:
* Responses API hosted MCP tool -- OPENAI'S SERVERS make the call, so
server_url must be reachable from the public internet, or reached via
OpenAI's Secure MCP Tunnel (outbound-only, no inbound firewall hole).
* Agents SDK MCPServerStdio -- YOUR process spawns the server locally.
No public endpoint, no gateway, no inbound anything. For a firewalled
Windows server this is by far the better fit, and we emit it first.
require_approval defaults to asking on every call. Leave it that way for
a suite that can write to an estate.
unverified: Whether OpenAI's tunnel-client ships a supported Windows binary/service.
The documented deployment patterns are Kubernetes and VM/systemd.

targets.label: n8n (MCP Client Tool node)
notes: NO STDIO. The MCP Client Tool node has an endpoint URL and a transport
(SSE, or HTTP Streamable from node v1.2), and no command/args properties
of any kind. The gateway is not an optimisation here, it is the only way.
One MCP Server credential per domain URL; one tool sub-node per domain.
Load only the domains a workflow needs -- n8n injects every tool schema
from every configured server into the prompt on EVERY invocation.
The suite ships its own guide at bConnect-MCP-main\docs\N8N.md.
unverified: Reports exist of the transport dropdown being ignored and SSE used
regardless, which breaks against a streamable-only server. Check the
behaviour of your n8n version before relying on the dropdown.

targets.label: Open WebUI
notes: Open WebUI has consumed MCP natively since v0.6.31, and NATIVE SUPPORT IS
STREAMABLE HTTP ONLY -- there is no stdio path. That is exactly what this
suite's gateway serves, so no mcpo bridge is needed on 0.6.31+.
Configured in the web UI (Admin Settings -> External Tools -> Add Server,
type 'MCP (Streamable HTTP)'), so there is no file to write. We emit the
URLs and the steps.
An mcpo config is also emitted for pre-0.6.31 installs: mcpo takes a
literal Claude-Desktop-shaped {"mcpServers": {...}} JSON via --config and
re-exposes it as OpenAPI, which Open WebUI consumes as a tool server.
If Open WebUI is containerised and the gateway is on this host, use
http://host.docker.internal:<port> rather than localhost.
unverified: The exact per-server URL path mcpo serves when driven by --config with
several servers. Widely reported as /<serverName>, and mcpo's own
/docs will tell you -- check it rather than trusting this note.

targets.label: Cursor
notes: Global alternative: %USERPROFILE%\.cursor\mcp.json.
Remote servers are declared by the PRESENCE of `url` (plus optional
`headers` / `auth`), with no `type` field in any documented example.
unverified: The docs' field table marks `type` as Required for stdio, and then every
documented example -- stdio and remote alike -- omits it. We follow the
examples and omit `type`. If a future Cursor build rejects that, the fix
is one line in this file: change stdioStyle to typed-stdio.
Whether Cursor accepts an explicit type on remote entries, and with what
values, is not documented at all.

targets.label: Continue (continue.dev)
notes: The odd one out: `mcpServers` here is a YAML LIST of objects, each
carrying its own `name:`, not a map keyed by server name. A config
translated field-for-field from any other host on this list is wrong.
We write a standalone BLOCK file under .continue/mcpServers/, which needs
the name/version/schema header. That is a whole new file, so there is no
existing YAML for us to re-serialise and no merge risk.
MCP is usable in AGENT mode only.
This is the natural target for a self-hosted Ollama model: Continue speaks
MCP and talks to a local model.
unverified: `type:` and `url:` appear on the MCP deep-dive page but are absent from
the config.yaml reference's property table. The stdio shape is confirmed
in both; the HTTP shape rests on the deep-dive page alone.
The legacy config.json MCP shape is not in the current docs at all.

targets.label: LibreChat
notes: Snippet, not a merge: librechat.yaml is a large hand-maintained file with
comments and anchors. Re-serialising it would destroy both. Paste the
emitted block under the top-level `mcpServers:` key.
The one host on this list that runs a LOCAL STDIO server directly AND
drives a self-hosted model -- so this is the reference target for the
'local LLM, no internet' case.
stdio servers run on the LIBRECHAT host. If LibreChat is in Docker, the
suite must be inside that container or on a mounted path; librechat.yaml
must be in the project root and mounted into the API container.
Pointing LibreChat at a private HTTP address may need allowedDomains /
allowedAddresses under the mcpSettings key.
unverified: Nothing was executed. LibreChat is not installed on this machine.

targets.label: Generic / any other MCP client
notes: The fallback that keeps this honest: the exact command line, argument by
argument, quoted for cmd and for POSIX, plus a portable mcpServers JSON
block. Any MCP client that can spawn a process or call a URL can be
configured from this, including ones that did not exist when this was
written.
The command line is the same one Claude Desktop is given, so if the
generic block does not work, neither does the verified target.
